speech.transcript: Your phone keyboard guesses the next word. Look at the three suggestions above it. An LLM does the same thing, but with almost all the text humans have ever written. LLM stands for "large language model." Large means billions of numbers inside it, called parameters. Language means it works with words. A model is just a pattern learner, not a database and not a thinking brain. Say you type, the capital of India is. The model answers New Delhi. It does not open a page. It produces the answer from patterns. It has seen millions of times. Ask about something rare and it still writes a smooth sentence. Training is simple to describe. It reads a huge pile of text. For every next word, it guesses, checks the answer, and nudges its numbers. A wrong guess is not a failure. It is the signal that moves the numbers. Repeat that billions of times. The trick is attention. When it reads a sentence, it weighs which words matter for the next one. Like guessing the next line of a song from the whole stanza, not just the last word. That is why a word's meaning can change with the sentence around it. At small scale, it is just autocomplete. At large scale, next word prediction starts to look like reasoning. The same machine can summarize a chapter, translate a message, or write code. It can also follow instructions and answer in your language. But it is still guessing. It can be confidently wrong because it predicts plausible text, not checked facts. Ask for a source and it may invent one. So verify anything important with a book or a trusted website. An LLM is a very well-trained next-word predictor. Useful, but not magic.
